newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn sees EMU deficit below 3 pct,analysts dubious.
newsitem.headline: Bonn sees EMU deficit below 3 pct,analysts dubious.

text.p: Germany's finance ministry on Tuesday denied a report that high joblessness had forced it to ratchet up its deficit forecast for 1997 to a level which would scupper its chances of qualifying legitimately for the euro.

A ministry spokesman dismissed a BBC report saying Bonn was now officially expecting a deficit at 3.5 percent of gross domestic product -- above the three percent reference level set in the Maastricht Treaty and Bonn's 2.9 percent forecast.
"The government's prognosis was in the annual economic report that came out three weeks ago," a spokesman said. "There is no reason to change the prognosis after three weeks."
Analysts, and markets, treated the BBC report sceptically -- scoffing at the idea Bonn would suddenly issue a forecast with such dramatic consequences for Europe's currency aims.
"If they did think of changing things, they wouldn't do it in February," said Alison Cottrell, economist at PaineWebber, adding that Bonn would normally wait until later in the year.
But many admitted the 3.5 percent figure itself was not an impossible outcome, given Germany's growing economic problems.

"Most analysts had never believed the government's earlier estimate of 2.5 percent and do not believe the current official 2.9 percent either," said Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs. "Most forecasts already fall in the three to 3.5 percent range."
Only 15 months ago Germany was virtuously lecturing other European Union members on reining in spending, tyrannising weaker EU members with its plans for a one percent deficit.
But it was forced to moderate its tone after finding itself exceeding the three percent Maastricht target in 1995 and 1996.

Shock data this month -- putting January's jobless at 4.66 million levels not seen since the depressions of the 1930's -- gave rise to a new horror scenario, in which Germany could fail to provide a benchmark for other countries' EMU qualification.

Countries which want to meld their currencies in the euro have to meet goals on budgets and debt, inflation and interest and exchange rates this year. Germany, as Europe's largest economy, is viewed as an absolutely essential founder member.

Although Europe could decide to bend the rules and go ahead with the project with Germany, even if it does not qualify according to the strict rules laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, this would make it very hard to exclude southern Mediterranean countries which have no stability track record.
The result could be a weak euro, lacking market confidence.
But for now, Bonn remains confident it will hit the target.

The finance ministry spokesman said January's surge in unemployment had not altered Bonn's expectation of meeting the EMU criteria, adding that much of the increase was a result of bad winter weather that idled many construction workers.
"The seasonally adjusted unemployment figure was about 200,000 higher than was expected..." he said. "The ministry expects a clear drop in unemployment this year."

But although economists agree January's jobless figure is heavily distorted by seasonal factors and likely to drop by March or April, they say the average for 1997 is likely to be higher than the assumption behind for Bonn's deficit forecast.

"It seems likely the latest projection from the federal government of 4.2 million unemployed on average for 1997 could be exceeded," Trinkaus Capital Management said, referring to a forecast made by Economic Minister Guenter Rexrodt last week.
"In our view that will mean the Maastricht deficit goal will not be met," Trinkaus added in a commentary.

Economists assess that an extra 100,000 unemployed per year adds 0.1 or 0.15 percentage points to the Maastricht deficit calculation, taking into account the additional benefit costs and likely losses in income tax revenues which result.

Armin Kayser at SBC Warburg said he currently expected a deficit figure of 3.3 percent by the end of the year, and argued that tax income losses, rather than joblessness itself was the main threat to the federal government's spending plan.
He added that tax income growth last year had fallen behind the expected complex ratio to economic growth last year and that there were signs this could happen again in 1997.
"The deficit forecast has already been increased by a disturbing amount," he said. "This was the lesson we learned from last year and it looks as if it will repeat itself."

On the implications for the euro's launch, Mayer at Goldman Sachs said he believed Germany would simply join the growing line of European nations which have opted to "fudge" their accounts, led by France with its now sanctioned use of pension fund transfers from France Telecom.

"I am still sticking to a forecast of 3.4 percent based on proper accounting," Mayer said. "But I think in the end the books will show 2.9 percent. The French example has established 0.5 percentage point as the allowed fudge."
